title: guest-tenant-preemption-oom-cascade-postmortem
content:
Summary:
On 2025-11-02 we observed a multi-host memory surge and host OOMs that temporarily reduced cluster capacity for the hosted inference fleet. The immediate trigger was a sequence of reserved-capacity tenant preemption events that caused unusually large KV-cache invalidations and concurrent background serialization retries. Those retries collided with continuous-batching changes introduced in the prior week, producing long-lived microbatches that pinned large token-prefix buffers and prevented normal eviction. The combined effect was memory amplification across several hosts and eventual OOMs on 5 hosts in the us-west-2 region.

Impact:
- ~12 minutes of elevated 95/99 latency for text-generation routes backed by model-x-1.
- 5 hosts OOMed and were replaced by autoscaler, causing temporary capacity reduction and a short spike in request queueing.
- ~4500 requests retried by clients over the 20-minute incident window.
- No customer data exfiltration or correctness regressions observed.

Detection and Alerting:
- First signal: internal host-memory-surge alert fired for a single host at 03:41 UTC (memory > 92%).
- Secondary: a host OOM event and kernel OOM-killer logs surfaced at 03:45 UTC; SRE pager triggered at 03:46 UTC.
- Observability gaps: KV-cache eviction rate metric was noisy and didn't cross its single-host alert threshold; there was no dedicated alert for concurrent preemption-induced serialization retries.

Timeline (high level):
- 03:37 UTC: Scheduled capacity rebalance for reserved-tenants triggered preemption on a pool of hosts to make room for higher-priority reserved jobs.
- 03:38–03:40 UTC: KV-cache nodes received mass invalidation calls due to tenant eviction; background serializer enqueues 400–600 invalidations per host instead of typical 20–40.
- 03:40 UTC: Continuous-batching snapshot introduced last week caused microbatching to prefer longer accumulation windows when in-flight KV misses exceed threshold T (regression from rollout r-2025-10-27).
- 03:41–03:45 UTC: Microbatches lengthened, KV eviction could not keep up; memory for prefix buffers amplified (estimated additional 20–30% per host).
- 03:45 UTC: Kernel OOMs occurred on 5 hosts; autoscaler started draining and replacing hosts.
- 03:56 UTC: Autoscaler achieved replacement host pool size; global routing fell back to lower-priority capacity for a brief period to maintain availability.
- 04:00 UTC: Incident declared resolved after no further OOMs and latency returned to baseline by 04:05 UTC.

Root cause (contributing factors):
1) Reserved-tenant preemption spike: the capacity rebalance produced an unusually dense window of preemptions that created a burst of KV invalidations. The rebalance scheduler is functioning but lacks smoothing for downstream invalidation load.
2) Background serialization retry behavior: on invalidation we serialize eviction events to durable store with aggressive retry/backoff policy; the policy was not adaptive to queue depth, so retries multiplied when the serializer lagged.
3) Continuous-batching regression: the recent change increased accumulation windows when KV-miss concurrency rose; this interacted poorly with the invalidation burst and caused microbatches to hold onto large prefix buffers longer than expected.
4) Observability gaps: no alert for serialization retry queue depth or unusually high invalidation bursts; batch length SLOs were only checked per-host as a percentile and didn't show the early spike.

Immediate mitigations taken during the incident:
- 03:47 UTC: Scaled down the reserved-tenant rebalance rate (disabled the aggressive window) via dynconfig flag to stop further preemptions. This immediately reduced new invalidations.
- 03:49 UTC: Throttled background serializer concurrency on the affected host pool (reduced workers from 8 -> 2) to limit competing memory allocations; this slowed progress but reduced amplification.
- 03:52 UTC: Rolled back the continuous-batching config from rollout r-2025-10-27 for the us-west-2 region to restore prior accumulation behavior.
- 03:58 UTC: Increased eviction aggressiveness by temporarily lowering the KV-cache soft-threshold to force earlier reclaim.
These mitigations prevented further OOMs and allowed the autoscaler to replace crashed hosts without re-triggering the cascade.

Root fix plan (short/medium/long term):
Short term (1–2 weeks):
- Add an adaptive backoff to the background serializer: when queue depth > X, switch to exponential backoff and reduce per-retry memory allocations. Owner: Marcus Liu. ETA: 2025-11-14.
- Add an emergency dynconfig that reduces reserved-tenant rebalance aggressiveness automatically if invalidation rate spikes above threshold. Owner: SRE runbook team. ETA: 2025-11-10.
- Revert continuous-batching default for all regions until full safety validation is added. Owner: Serving runtime oncall lead. ETA: 2025-11-05.

Medium term (1–2 months):
- Implement a preemption smoothing layer in the capacity rebalance scheduler that spreads tenant preemptions over a sliding window to avoid burst invalidations. Owner: Platform-engineering. ETA: 2025-12-20.
- Rework KV-cache eviction to support low-latency path for mass-invalidations (bulk eviction path that uses batched metadata updates instead of per-key serialization). Owner: Serving runtime team. ETA: 2025-12-15.
- Add a simulator test that can reproduce preemption + eviction + batching interactions at scale (load test in staging). Owner: Applied ML infra. ETA: 2025-12-01.

Long term (3–6 months):
- Move the background serializer to a backpressure-aware queue that signals upstream (batching) to reduce accumulation when serializer is lagging. Owner: Serving runtime + Infra. ETA: 2026-02-01.
- Instrument and expose KV invalidation burst metrics and create automated runbook triggers for dynconfig throttles. Owner: Observability. ETA: 2026-01-15.

Runbook updates (what to change now):
- New triage checklist item: if a host memory-surge alert coincides with scheduled reserved-tenant rebalance, immediately check invalidation_rate_per_sec and serializer_queue_depth. If both trending up, flip dynconfig to throttle preemption and reduce serializer concurrency.
- Add a one-click dynconfig to revert continuous-batching rollout per region.
- Add dashboard panel for "KV invalidation burst" with per-pool heatmap and alert at 10x baseline.

Testing and validation tasks added to CI/CD:
- Add unit tests for serializer adaptive-backoff logic.
- Add chaos test in staging: inject simultaneous preemptions on a reserved pool and validate no host memory spike > 85%.
- Add e2e regression test for continuous-batching config that asserts microbatch hold time distribution remains within historical baselines under KV-miss storms.

Action items (owners and due dates):
- Marcus Liu: implement serializer adaptive backoff and add unit tests. Due 2025-11-14.
- SRE runbook team: build dynconfig throttles and one-click rollback scripts. Due 2025-11-10.
- Serving runtime: rollback continuous-batching global default and run safety validation. Due 2025-11-05.
- Observability: add invalidation burst metric and dashboard panel. Due 2025-11-21.
- Platform-engineering: design preemption smoothing proposal (RFC). Due 2025-11-28.

Lessons learned / retrospective notes:
- Configuration changes that touch accumulation windows can have non-obvious memory amplification when combined with concurrent metadata operations (invalidations). We need more integration tests that exercise these orthogonal subsystems together.
- Autoscaler replacement masked the systemic problem — hosts replaced but the underlying trigger (rebalance burst) could have retriggered the cascade if not stopped. Auto-remediation should consider downstream load effects before scaling.
- Observability must expose not just percentiles but absolute event rates (e.g., invalidations/sec) and queue depths; these are early predictors of resource exhaustion.
- Runbook clarity: the oncall had to consult three separate playbooks (rebalance, kv-cache, batching) to cobble together a remediation; we must unify the steps into a single incident play.

Communication notes:
- Customer-facing: SRE -> Customer Success drafted a short note emphasizing availability maintained, brief latency impact, and that root cause was internal capacity reshaping behavior. No customers reported data loss.
- Internal: postmortem will be shared with Serving runtime, Platform engineering, Product (Dedicated), and Observability teams.

Appendix (evidence snippets):
- Kernel OOM logs (excerpt): "oom_kill_process: pid 4321 comm serializer_worker invoked oom-killer"
- Monitoring graph ids: host-memory-surge-2025-11-02-graph-7 (attached in Confluence link)
- Relevant PRs: github.com/redwood/inference/pull/4891 (continuous-batching change)

Open questions:
- Should reserved-tenant rebalance be moved off-host (centralized planning) to avoid correlated invalidations?
- Is there a hard lower bound on memory amplification from prefix buffering that needs a platform-level cap?

Next steps:
- Owners begin short-term mitigations immediately; SRE lead to schedule a cross-team incident review meeting w/c 2025-11-10 to walk plan and accept actions.

Notes to self (oncall diary style):
- This one felt like a multi-factor race: aggressive scheduler + noisy serializer + subtle batching change. The rollback and dynconfig throttle stopped the bleeding quickly once we identified the rebalance as the upstream signal. Keep an eye on the staging chaos test results once implemented — if that fails we'll need a hotfix for the serializer to be safer by default.

End of postmortem.
